title: Attacking Overload Against Back Five
definition: A tactical adjustment where a team commits additional players to the final third to create numerical superiority against a low defensive block of five.
content: When opponents defend in a back five to neutralize a team's central width, the attacking side must increase risk to break the deadlock. This involves the left-sided midfielder (often a pivot or box-to-box player) surging forward into the half-space rather than inverting to maintain a double pivot. Simultaneously, the full-back on that side pushes extremely high, effectively becoming a wide midfielder. This shifts the team shape from a standard 4-3-3 or 4-2-3-1 into a 3-1-6 or similar structure in the final third. The objective is to create a local numerical overload (e.g., 6v5) to exploit the gaps between the opponent's back five and their midfield line. While this approach generates high-quality chances through fluid movement and structure, it leaves the team vulnerable to counter-attacks if the press is bypassed, as only one central midfielder remains to protect the defensive line. This tactic requires high technical quality and pressing intensity to recover possession quickly.
example_questions: How can we create enough space to score when the other team parks five defenders in the box?
Their back five is so compact that we cannot get through the middle, what is the best way to break them down?
As a forward, should I stay wide to stretch their back five or drift inside to create a numerical advantage in the box?
We keep shooting from distance against low blocks, how do we get more players into the final third to create real chances?
